Morning update...
Latest satellite data shows an expansive area of cooling cloud tops
across northern Indiana as robust thunderstorms develop. This is the
second feature noted below. The evolution of this feature ahead of
the main line will play an important role in the higher-end scenario
for today. If this complex survives into the local area, this would
nudge the higher wind threat farther south. Wherever the northern
boundary of the highest instability resides, that will be the
northern extent of the more significant wind threat. More
specifically, this would decrease the potential for the significant
winds later today for locations like west-central Ohio into central 
and south- central Ohio. Depending on how far south it advances, the
threat could be limited to southeast Indiana, southwest Ohio, and
portions of northern Kentucky. Check for updates throughout the day!

Previous discussion (3:29 AM)...
KEY MESSAGE 1) Now that the late evening and early overnight 
thunderstorm complex has shifted southeast of the region, the 
northern half of the area is currently in a stable cold pool air 
mass, while the southern half is still considerable unstable. 
Thunderstorms are beginning to form along a stalled boundary 
currently placed across northern Indiana. If these thunderstorms 
attempt to move southeast, they will encounter the cold pool air mass
previously mentioned. These storms would struggle to organize as a 
result. Trends will be monitored over the next few hours, but this is
first feature which could play an important role in today's 
significant wind threat potential. 

The second feature is across southern Wisconsin and northern
Illinois. Near the northern tip of the low-level jet, thunderstorms
are beginning to develop. To the east and south of these storms,
undisturbed energy remains. While this is ahead of the better forcing
associated with the shortwave, the available energy to the south
would give it a much better chance to evolve into a more organized
storm complex into the morning hours. 

If these two features remain on the weaker side, confidence would
become very high that the local area would see a widespread, 
significant damaging wind event later this afternoon and evening. The
second feature has the better chance of organizing, therefore it 
would likely have the biggest role to play in altering local impacts 
from the higher-end scenario. There is also the potential where this
feature and the main event combine as they approach the local area. 

As SPC notes in their discussion, all environmental parameters are
in place for a widespread, potentially significant damaging wind
event across the area. The timing is also optimal for the local area,
moving through during the peak of the diurnal instability (afternoon
into evening). Damaging wind gusts of 75+ mph are likely if a well-
organized MCS can develop and then move through the area. The major
limiting factor would be any earlier development ahead of this main
event. Despite the focus being on the more widespread damaging wind
event, embedded tornadoes within the squall-line would also be
possible, especially on the northern segment of the MCS. Large hail
could also occur in the deepest thunderstorms. 

KEY MESSAGE 2)
Morning update...Flash flood watch expanded for the entire area.

Previous discussion (3:29 AM)...
The best chance for flash flooding across the northern portion of 
the area would be if multiple rounds of thunderstorms occur later 
this morning and through the afternoon. Then, if an organized MCS 
moves through, multiple inches would have accumulated over this 
region. 

Of more increasing concern, after the MCS moves through, moisture
will continue to move into the region from the southwest. Back
building of thunderstorms along the stretched outflow will focus a
flash flood threat over a portion of the area. This activity could
continue well into Wednesday as the front stalls over southern
portions of the area. SPC HREF LPMM does support this potential over
south-central and southern Ohio, but there is a growing signal for
southeast Indiana, southwest Ohio and northern Kentucky (some of
these counties are outside the flood watch). Because this threat may
not evolve until later tonight and into Wednesday, the flood watch 
has not been extended to include these areas quite yet. However, it 
may be needed later today as confidence increases. If a back-building
scenario can develop, localized amounts of 5-7" are plausible as seen
from earlier events in Perry County OH this evening.


KEY MESSAGE 3)

some breaks are possible. This is largely due to a ridge of high
